name: dauphinois
instructions:
Classical french potato gratin — thinly sliced potatoes and/or turnips baked in garlic-infused cream with nutmeg. Cheese is NOT necessary (I've tested with gruyère; the traditional cheese-less version is arguably better — see CHEESE note). Breadcrumbs on top as an optional presentation crust.

SERVES 6-8. 9x13 dish or oval gratin.

=== INGREDIENTS ===

- 2 lb POTATOES (golden or russet) AND/OR TURNIPS — any ratio works, including pure potato or pure turnip. Peel and slice VERY THINLY (~1/8 inch — mandoline ideal).
- 2 cups heavy whipping cream
- 1 cup whole milk
- 4 cloves garlic (2 to rub the dish, 2 sliced thin for the cream)
- 1/4 tsp freshly grated nutmeg
- 1 tsp salt (adjust to taste)
- freshly ground black pepper
- 1 tbsp butter, softened (for greasing the dish)
- OPTIONAL: 1 to 1 1/2 cups grated gruyère cheese (I've tested with it and don't think it's necessary — see CHEESE note)
- OPTIONAL: 1/2 cup breadcrumbs for presentation crust (oil-spray before uncovered bake — see BREADCRUMBS note)

=== PROCEDURE ===

1. PREHEAT the oven to 350°F.
2. PREP THE DISH: rub the inside of a 9x13 (or oval gratin) baking dish with 2 cloves of garlic (halved). Butter the dish generously with the softened butter.
3. INFUSE THE CREAM: in a saucepan, combine the heavy cream, milk, thinly sliced garlic (2 remaining cloves), nutmeg, salt, and a generous grind of black pepper. Bring to a bare simmer over medium-low heat — don't boil. Remove from heat and let steep 5 min. Fish out and discard the garlic slices.
4. LAYER THE POTATOES: arrange the sliced potatoes in overlapping rows in the buttered dish (like fish scales). Fill the dish evenly.
5. POUR THE CREAM OVER: pour the infused cream evenly over the potatoes — it should come up nearly to the top of the potatoes (not fully submerging).
6. BAKE COVERED at 350°F for ~45-55 min — use a REAL GLASS-LIDDED CASSEROLE DISH for the steam seal (foil is inadequate; see COVERAGE note).
7. UNCOVER for the last 15-20 min to develop the golden crust. Optional: scatter breadcrumbs across the top before uncovering and OIL-SPRAY THEM for browning (see BREADCRUMBS note). Total bake ~60-75 min. Done when cream bubbles around the edges, top is deeply golden, and a knife slides through the potatoes/turnips at the center without resistance.
8. REST 10-15 min before serving — the cream needs to reabsorb.
notes:
Classical french potato gratin. Comes from the Dauphiné region of southeastern France.

=== CHEESE — TESTED WITH GRUYÈRE, NOT NECESSARY ===

I've gratinéed this with gruyère (per Julia Child + most home-cook versions). It's not necessary. The dish reads fine — arguably better — without the cheese: cream + potato/turnip + garlic + nutmeg leads cleanly, and the cheese layer competes with rather than extends the dairy register.

This lines up with the STRICTLY TRADITIONAL FRENCH DAUPHINOIS (no cheese — that's what distinguishes dauphinois from GRATIN SAVOYARD, which canonically has gruyère). Turns out the traditionalists were right on this one.

Gruyère moved to secondary — add it if you specifically want the cheese-forward version, but don't reach for it by default.

=== BREADCRUMBS (SECONDARY) — PRESENTATION ADD ===

For a golden crust on top (visual improvement over just the cream-and-potato bake), scatter breadcrumbs across the surface after removing the lid for the final 15-20 min uncovered bake. OIL-SPRAY THE BREADCRUMBS BEFORE BAKING — otherwise they stay pale and dry instead of turning deeply golden.

Presentation add only; not part of the classical dish. But cleaner and simpler than cheese if you want a browned top.

=== POTATO CHOICE — GOLDEN OR RUSSET ===

Both work. GOLDEN POTATOES (yukon gold) hold their shape better and give a slightly waxier, more creamy-inside result. RUSSETS break down more, releasing starch that thickens the cream naturally — some argue this is the more classical result. Pick either.

Peel them either way — the skins get chewy and dark in the long bake and read wrong here.

=== SLICED TURNIPS (PRIMARY) — ANY POTATO-TURNIP RATIO WORKS ===

Turnips add a lot to this dish — promoted to primary. Any potato-to-turnip ratio works, including PURE POTATO or PURE TURNIP. Peel and slice to the same ~1/8 inch; alternate layers if mixing.

WALKED BACK FROM 2:1 REQUIREMENT: earlier notes suggested a 2:1 potato:turnip ratio was necessary for the starch to thicken the cream properly. That's not true — turnips work at any ratio, including alone. The cream sets fine either way; the turnip-only version reads lighter and more vegetal, the potato-only version reads more starchy-classical, and mixed ratios sit anywhere between.

=== SLICE VERY THIN — MANDOLINE IF YOU CAN ===

~1/8 inch is the target. Uniform thickness matters more than absolute thinness. A mandoline is the easiest way to get consistency. Uneven slices cook unevenly, leaving you with some pieces still firm while others are mush.

=== INFUSE THE CREAM BEFORE POURING ===

The brief simmer of cream + milk + garlic + nutmeg + salt + pepper (5 min steep) distributes flavor through the liquid before it hits the potatoes. Skipping this step and just pouring cold cream leaves the seasoning uneven — some bites will taste of nothing while others hit a raw-garlic pocket.

=== NO OIL — JUST BUTTER THE PAN, CREAM IS THE SAUCE ===

Interestingly, no oil in this recipe. Butter goes on the dish (rubbed with garlic first) for grease and flavor; cream is the sauce. Olive oil, vegetable oil, or any other cooking fat would clash with the dairy-forward register and doesn't belong. Butter + cream + milk is the whole fat stack.

=== CREAM AND MILK, NOT JUST CREAM ===

Some versions use all cream. That's fine but reads heavier. The 2:1 cream-to-milk ratio lightens the dish just enough to still be rich without being punishing. If you only have cream, use it (dilute with a bit of milk if you want).

=== BAKE AT 350°F (NOT HIGHER — CREAM SPLITS AT 400°F) ===

350°F is the target. 400°F is TOO HOT for the cream — it can SPLIT / break at that temperature, leaving you with grainy dairy solids and pooled fat instead of a smooth cream-thickened gratin. Even 375°F is on the edge. Keep it at 350°F throughout.

60-75 min is the bake window. Signals for done: cream bubbling around the edges (not just the center), top deeply golden, knife slides through the potatoes at the center without resistance.

=== COVERAGE IS THE HARDEST PART — USE A REAL GLASS-LIDDED CASSEROLE DISH ===

Getting enough steam trapped over the potatoes to actually cook them through is the hardest part of this recipe. The potatoes need steam from above to cook uniformly; without it, the top potatoes stay firm while the bottom braises in cream.

USE A REAL GLASS COVERED CASSEROLE DISH. Aluminum foil is CUMBERSOME and always seems INCOMPLETE — it doesn't seal well enough to trap the steam properly, and shaping it around an irregular dish rim is a pain. A glass-lidded casserole dish gives you a real seal and lets you check progress without breaking it.

If you don't have a glass-lidded dish, foil is the fallback but expect uneven cooking. A heavy dutch oven with a lid is another option, though the shape isn't ideal for the gratin format.

UNCOVER FOR THE LAST 15-20 MIN: to develop the golden crust on top after the potatoes are cooked through.

=== REST BEFORE SERVING ===

10-15 min out of the oven lets the cream reabsorb into the potatoes. Serving straight out of the oven means the cream runs everywhere on the plate; a proper rest gives you a set gratin that holds its slice.

=== PAIRINGS ===

Rich enough to be a main; classical as a side alongside:
- French-beef-and-mushroom-stew (variant A — Julia's Boeuf Bourguignon — this is a canonical pairing)
- Chicken-with-vinegar or chicken-piccata (starch alongside a lighter chicken dish)
- Coq au vin (traditional french chicken braise)
- Roasted or grilled meats in general

Goes particularly well anywhere a starch would be traditional — this replaces or upgrades mashed potatoes.
original_chef: Classical french regional dish (Dauphiné). This version leans on Julia Child's cheese-on-top approach; the strictly-traditional french dauphinois skips the cheese entirely (see notes).
